newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany contains swine fever, pig prices soar.
newsitem.headline: Germany contains swine fever, pig prices soar.

text.p: Swine fever outbreaks in Germany are receding while the disease is lingering in the Netherlands, German farm sources said on Wednesday.
Pigmeat prices in Germany have soared in recent weeks amid Dutch supply reductions, benefiting domestic pig farmers, who usually battle against Dutch competition.
Consumer prices are expected to stay firm at least until the autumn.
A veterinary expert at the Bonn agriculture ministry said the number of herds affected in April was down at nine from 29 in March, which compared with 23 in February and 13 in January.
Germany in a preventative cull had slaughtered around 85,000 animals so far this year and any further outbreaks were likely to be small and isolated.
Key producing regions such as Lower Saxony were mostly unaffected.
The Netherlands had culled around one million animals by the end of April and on Monday won European Union approval for the subsidised slaughter of an additional 500,000 piglets.
The contagious disease hurts the Netherlands most because the outbreaks are happening in areas with a dense animal population.
German meat market analysts said Dutch export availability to other EU countries had fallen by 40 percent.
While normally three quarters of German imports come from the Netherlands, Dutch buyers were now making inquiries in Germany.

In another development adding to tightness, Danish pig exports had been redirected from Germany to Japan, where imports from traditional supplier Taiwan were sharply down because of an outbreak of foot and mouth hog disease.
Slaughter pigs here last cost 4.35 marks per kilo carcass weight, compared with 2.77 marks on average in January.
